Hello fellow DIY-ers! This weekend I will be completely sanding and refinishing our wood floors! While I’ve read (and watched) up on this topic extensively, I wanted to come here to see if there are any last-minute gems you DIY-ers may be able to bestow upon me. I will be refinishing somewhere in the ballpark of 700-900 sqft and will be working on what I believe to be Red Oak floors (Floor picture 1). These floors are (presumably) original to the house which is approaching 70 years old and there is not much finish left on them; high traffic areas are essentially bare and will readily absorb water. Given this, my process will be as follows:

  1. Remove quarter-rounds from base molding.
  2. Look for and sink any protruding nails.
  3. Start off sanding with 32 grit (floor sander --> hand sander --> sand paper for corners before moving to another grit).
  4. Apply wood putty to any crevices/spaces between boards.
  5. Sand with 50 or 60 grit.
  6. Sand with 80 grit.
  7. Sand with 100 or 120 grit (this step optional depending on how long everything has taken thus far).
  8. After cleaning with a shop vac between grits, vacuum entire area thoroughly (including other rooms, window sills, ceiling fans, door trim, etc.).
  9. Go over floors once or twice with a damp (not wet) mop.
  10. Pass out and hope for at least 8 hours of sleep.
  11. Put on clean shoes.
  12. Wipe floor clean with mineral spirits and white rags until there are no more visible particulates or discoloration resulting from wiping.
  13. Apply floor finish (using an interesting tung oil-based product called Waterlox original, supposed to be awesome stuff, worthy of its own post) with lambskin applicator per manufacturer instructions.
  14. Apply additional two coats depending on drying conditions (possibly a fourth if I’m wrong about the floors being oak or I needs more delicious gloss).
  15. Leave it be for the next week or two while ensuring proper ventilation for curing (box fan in window for cross-ventilation, turn ceiling fans off to avoid “skin” developing on a coat).

Is there anything I’ve left off, might be forgetting, or may want to reconsider? I also still have a couple questions I haven’t been able to resolve using my Google-Fu, so if anyone has experience here or is otherwise at liberty to provide an answer, that would be great!

  1. I will not be using a drum sander. I’ve narrowed it down to either a “traditional” random orbital sander (3-4 small circular discs) or a square buff sander (one big square, not sure if it’s considered random, but it’s certainly an orbital sander). These seem to be used interchangeably as the alternative to a drum sander. Based on what I’ve read, a random orbital sander might be slightly quicker, but it appears both return similar results though a square buff will sometimes get closer to walls/corners. Is there any difference between the two which I might want to consider? If not, I’ll make my decision based on the cost per square foot of sand paper discs/squares.

  2. Sand paper/discs. How many discs/squares can I expect to go through (assuming I did a fantastic job of removing nails…), or rather, how many square feet can I expect to cover per replacement assuming red oak floors? Right now I’m planning just buy way more than I think I’ll need (based on what other first-timers have reported) and return whatever I don’t use since returning to the hardware store for extras will be time consuming.

  3. Floor picture 2 Am I right in guessing I have Red Oak floors?? I didn’t have the sense to ask as a first time home buyer :( In return for your help, I promise pretty pictures after the project has been completed.
Refinishing old floors this weekend, looking for advice!

Hard to tell from a pic, but yes, that is most likely Red Oak. 2 1/4" tounge-and-groove x 3/4", varied lengths to be exact.

Is the Waterlox water or oil based?

As I understand it (and feel free anyone to correct me if I'm totally wrong), it's a weird hybrid of both. It's a tung-oil based finish dissolved in mineral spirits, so it's applied like a water-based finish. It's an interesting product entirely worthy of its own post, but you can find more info here: http://www.waterlox.com/tung-oil/what-is-waterlox
Extremely thorough FAQ section. Check out the section on wood fillers.

Yeah, their website is really great. Almost everything people seemed to converge on was posted somewhere in their FAQ or product manual. I didn't see the part about the wood fillers, thanks so much for drawing my attention! I just have regular Elmer's brand wood filler, but heard about a product called Woodwise, ever heard of it? Anyway, I might forego wood filler entirely; my planks are generally very close; I just saw a lot of other people (including professionals) going through that process as a matter of practice.

If I find any large cracks, I'll definitely test out the filler with waterlox in a closeted area first. So glad I made this post!

The most important part of that was that Waterlox is a penetrating finish, not a top-side sealing varnish. Wood floors move a lot under temperature/moisture variations, and a solid blob of fill can pop out eventually. Also, fills take stain uniformly, and tend to stand out when stained as a solid block of light color against darker and grainy wood. I try to keep the fill to nail holes and knots that are cracking, leaving the natural gaps in the wood for the sander only. A great tip is to rub some sawdust from the sanding into small cracks before you oil it, instead of wood fill.

Go easy with the lower grit sanding, because you can make your floor really uneven. Don't even worry about getting all of the finish off with the lowest grit, everything will be gone by the time you're done. Vacuum often to keep the sandpaper from clogging, and so you can see the effects of your labor. Also, use a high quality wood putty. I had a boss buy some really cheap crap once, it was popping out before we even started finishing the floors.

Edit: 32 grit also seems awfully low, especially since your floors look pretty smooth. Maybe start out with 40 grit.

Edit 2: Now that I think about it, 40 grit might even be too low. The really heavy grit is for new floors, to even up the individual boards.

Interesting, you think 32 is too low even considering I won't be using a drum sander? I've read multiple counts of people suggesting not to skip the lower grains, 32 is the lowest applicator I generally carried before 50
I suppose it does depend on the sander. Just be careful with the heavier grits, because they remove a large amount of material very quickly.

Here's a simple fix I made to make that page not as bright as the sun:

Download Stylish:
Stylish for Google Chrome
Stylish for Firefox

Click the specify button and change the dropdown to "URLs matching the regexp" and set it to https?://(|www.)voat.co/(?!/v/*)

Copy below into the big box. 

html, body { background: #292929 !important; }
#header, #header-container { background: #333333 !important; border-color: #222 !important; }
.panel-info>.panel-heading { background: #2e2e2e; background: -webkit-linear-gradient(top,#2e2e2e,#2b2b2b); background: -moz-linear-gradient(top,#2e2e2e,#2b2b2b); background: -ms-linear-gradient(top,#2e2e2e,#2b2b2b); background: -o-linear-gradient(top,#2e2e2e,#2b2b2b); border-color: #272727; color: #ebebeb; }
.panel-body { background-color: #292929; color: #ebebeb; border: none; }
.panel { background: none; }

Make sure to put a name in the box on the left and then save

In firefox:

go to about:addons, click "user Styles", click write new styles.

Enter a name in the name field and then copy the below stuff into the big box and then save.
